Cling
KLING
v.
Old English clingan, “to shrink, wither, hold fast.” Renders the Hebrew dābaq, “to stick, cling, cleave,” in its devotional-adhesion uses, and the Greek kollaō, “to join, glue, stick to.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To cling, in Scripture, is the devotional adhesion of the soul to the LORD—the act by which the saint, having tasted that the LORD is good, refuses to let Him go and binds himself to Him with the whole weight of his trust, love, and life. The Hebrew dābaq is the great clinging verb of the Old Testament. It is used of the husband cleaving to his wife (Gen 2:24); it is the verb of Ruth’s loyalty to Naomi (and Ruth clave unto her); but its supreme use is devotional: that thou mayest love the LORD thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days (Deut 30:20); my soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me (Ps 63:8—the verb is dābaq, ‘to cling’); but ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day (Deut 4:4). The Greek kollaō carries the same picture into the New Testament: cleave to that which is good (Rom 12:9); and the verb stands behind the warning that he which is joined to an harlot is one body (1 Cor 6:16) and the promise that he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit (1 Cor 6:17). The clinging is therefore covenantal, exclusive, and total: the soul refuses any rival adhesion that would split its loyalty, and presses against the LORD as the only object worthy of so weighted a bond. The picture is bodily: the child who will not be pried from the parent, the bride who holds fast to the bridegroom, the climber whose whole weight is on the rope. Clinging is the saint’s posture in temptation (when nothing but the LORD will hold), in suffering (when the LORD is the only stable ground), in prosperity (when the soul that does not cling to Him will cling to His gifts and lose Him), and in death (when the clinging soul is met by the right hand that upholds and is brought safe through the valley to the everlasting hills).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CLING as to adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast upon, especially by winding round or embracing; figuratively, to adhere to a person or cause with strong affection.

expand to see more

CLING, v.i. — 1. To adhere closely; to stick; to hold fast upon, especially by winding round or embracing; as, the tendril of a vine clings to its support; the infant clings to its mother. 2. To adhere closely with affection; to be devoted; to follow closely. Cleave to that which is good (Rom 12:9).

CLINGING, ppr. — Adhering closely; sticking to; holding fast.

📖 Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 30:20 — "That thou mayest love the LORD thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days."

Psalm 63:8 — "My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me."

Romans 12:9 — "Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good."

1 Corinthians 6:17 — "But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Clinging to the LORD is corrupted by the diversified-loyalty register of late-modern faith—the soul that holds the LORD as one bond among many rather than as the supreme bond—and by the displacement clinging that fastens itself to His gifts (career, family, comfort, the affirming church) rather than to Him.

expand to see more

Clinging in the biblical sense is exclusive: the soul refuses any rival adhesion that would split its loyalty. The diversified-loyalty register of contemporary faith corrupts this by treating the LORD as one of several bonds the believer maintains—alongside career, family, identity-group, political tribe, friends, hobbies—rather than as the supreme bond that orders all the rest. The result is a faith that does not cling but merely affiliates: present at services, present in profession, present in the categories of self-identification, but not bound to the LORD with the whole weight of the soul. The biblical verb is sharper. Ruth clave unto Naomi at real cost (her people, her gods, her future); the saints who cleave unto the LORD their God are alive every one of you this day; the verb is exclusive because the LORD is alone worthy of an exclusive bond. Diversified loyalty is not modesty about devotion; it is the soul’s refusal to be bound to its proper object.

The more subtle corruption is displacement clinging: the soul attaches itself, often unawares, to the gifts of the LORD rather than to the LORD Himself. The career becomes the bond; the spouse becomes the bond; the children become the bond; the comfortable house, the affirming church, the satisfying ministry, the political project become the bond. The gifts are good; the displacement is the corruption. When the gift is taken or threatened—the career lost, the spouse buried, the child wayward, the comfort stripped—the soul that clung to the gift discovers the substitution and is shaken to its foundations, because the foundation it had built upon was not the LORD but His provision. The recovery is the deliberate transfer of the clinging back to its proper object: thou art my portion, O LORD; whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever. The clinging that survives the loss of every gift is the clinging that was bound to the Giver.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dābaq (to stick, cling, cleave) in its devotional uses (Deut 30:20; Ps 63:8); Greek kollaō (to join, glue, stick to) in Rom 12:9 and 1 Cor 6:17—the soul’s exclusive devotional adhesion to the LORD as supreme bond.

expand to see more

Hebrew dābaq (H1692) — to stick, cling, cleave; the great devotional-adhesion verb (Deut 4:4; 10:20; 11:22; 13:4; 30:20; Josh 22:5).

Greek kollaō (G2853) — to join, glue, stick to (Rom 12:9; 1 Cor 6:17; Acts 5:13; 17:34).

Greek proskollaō (G4347) — to join closely to (Matt 19:5; Mark 10:7; Eph 5:31).

Hebrew rādap ‘achar’ (H7291) — to follow hard after; cousin verb of the chasing pursuit that clinging produces.

Usage

"Biblical clinging is covenantal, exclusive, and total—the soul refuses any rival adhesion that would split its loyalty."

"Displacement clinging fastens to the gifts rather than the Giver; the loss of the gift discovers the substitution and shakes the soul to its foundations."

"My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me—the saint clings, and the upholding hand answers."
